# Umbrella Cockatoo

The Umbrella Cockatoo is a large white cockatoo named for its dramatic, fan-shaped crest. Its social intelligence and expressive nature come with substantial demands for attention, space, noise management and long-term planning.

Scientific nameCacatua alba

Typical adult sizeAbout 46 cm long; commonly around 500–700 g, with individual variation.

Lifetime planningPotentially several decades; plan for a long-lived bird without assuming a maximum age.

## Overview and appearance

Umbrella Cockatoos are mostly white, with a broad rounded crest that fans open when the bird is excited, curious or alarmed. Yellow colouring appears beneath the wings and tail. They have a strong dark bill and a robust body, and need an environment built for a large, dexterous parrot.

The species is native to Indonesia’s northern Moluccan islands. As a companion it retains a need to climb, explore, chew and communicate. White plumage and an affectionate reputation should not be mistaken for a decorative or low-maintenance pet. Cockatoos also produce powder down, a household consideration.

## Temperament and social needs

Umbrella Cockatoos are often highly interactive and expressive, but each bird has preferences and limits. Constant close contact is not a sustainable care plan. Teach calm independent play from the start and provide a reliable routine that balances companionship, foraging and undisturbed rest.

A bird may use its beak when excited, uncertain or seeking space. Learn its signals and arrange handling around choice, not pressure. Adults should supervise all interactions with children, and every family member needs consistent guidance about boundaries and safe contact.

## Typical adult size

An adult is roughly 46 cm long and commonly weighs about 500–700 g. These are broad reference ranges. A large, sturdy enclosure with room to climb and stretch is essential, along with a secure bird-safe area for supervised exercise. Beak strength and escape skills require robust fittings and thoughtful room preparation.

## Expected lifespan and long-term care

Umbrella Cockatoos can be long-lived, with a care horizon of several decades. No general lifespan figure guarantees an individual’s longevity. Consider future guardianship, changing circumstances and the ability to provide continuing daily care before committing.

## Talking and vocalisation

This cockatoo has a powerful voice and can make loud contact calls. Some individuals imitate sounds, but speech varies and should never be promised. Sound is a normal part of parrot communication; think carefully about neighbours and the household’s tolerance before choosing the species.

## Intelligence and reward-based training

Intelligence and curiosity make positive-reinforcement training and enrichment important. Practise voluntary carrier entry, stepping to a perch and settling on a station in brief sessions. Offer safe foraging and chewing tasks. Without satisfying activity, a bird may redirect its energy into persistent calling or destructive chewing; meeting needs is more useful than punishment.

## Diet and nutrition

Feed a balanced, suitable formulated diet with a variety of fresh vegetables and thoughtfully measured fruit and treats. Do not rely on seed mixes or high-fat treats as the main food. Discuss an individual feeding plan, body condition and diet transitions with an avian veterinarian; routine supplements should not be added without advice.

## Housing, exercise and enrichment

Provide spacious secure accommodation, varied perches, safe exercise and durable chewable enrichment. Rotate activities to encourage exploration and food-searching. Inspect toys and fittings often. Plan for powder down, cleaning and ventilation as part of choosing where the bird will spend time.

## Is an Umbrella Cockatoo a fit?

This species may fit a well-prepared home with time for daily social contact, independent enrichment, noise tolerance and substantial long-term resources. It is not generally an easy first parrot. The bird must not be expected to fill a person’s entire social life; a sustainable routine benefits both bird and household.

Ask about the individual’s history, handling, diet, vocal habits and daily schedule. Consider room, neighbours, cleaning, safe access to exercise and a plan for care if circumstances change. Confirm current individual availability directly: this educational profile is not a stock statement.
